title: Thanksgiving: no closing bell today
text: U.S. stock markets stayed closed all day for Thanksgiving, so there was no close to report. The prices on this page are still from Wednesday. That day SPY, the S&P 500 fund, ended down 0.29% and QQQ, the Nasdaq 100 fund, ended down 0.65%. Trading comes back Friday, but stocks close early at 1 p.m. Eastern time. Fewer people trade on short days, so prices can move more than usual. Next week brings new data on jobs and the run up to the Fed's December meeting.

title: AI chip makers are still far from their highs
text: The five AI supplier companies on our list are, on average, about 40% below their highest price of the past year. The four AI giants (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta) are about 21% below on average. The suppliers also have higher risk scores: about 6.7 out of 10 on average, versus about 4.4 for the giants. Suppliers sell the chips and gear, so their sales can rise and fall faster when the giants change their spending plans.

title: Fewer Thanksgiving weekend shoppers expected
text: A survey by the National Retail Federation, a group for store owners, expects about 183 million people to shop over Thanksgiving weekend. That is about 2% fewer than it expected last year. Black Friday is still the most popular day. Shopping matters to stocks because people buying things is the biggest part of the U.S. economy. It can affect companies like Amazon.

title: Interest rates are still the big story
text: The 10 year Treasury yield averaged 5.13% in October, up from 4.09% a year earlier. That is the interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow for 10 years. Inflation was 3.8% in October, and minutes from the Fed's last meeting showed most officials expect more rate hikes. When safe bonds pay more, some investors move money out of stocks, especially fast growing tech stocks.

title: Lesson 69: What is consumer spending?
text: Consumer spending is all the money regular people spend on things like food, clothes, phones, trips and haircuts. In the U.S. it is the biggest part of the whole economy, about two thirds of it. That is why investors watch Black Friday and holiday shopping so closely. When people spend more, stores and the companies that supply them usually sell more and earn more. When people get worried and spend less, those companies can earn less. Careful, though: if prices are rising, people can spend more dollars and still buy fewer things. So a bigger spending number is not always good news.

title: What this update covers
text: Markets were closed today, so prices, 52 week ranges, beta and company size are from Wednesday's close, from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP). Analyst price targets and company ratios come from FMP for NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace; our free plan does not include them for Broadcom, Vertiv, Rocket Lab, Eli Lilly or Intuitive Surgical. The 10 year Treasury yield comes from Alpha Vantage. News comes from the sources linked on each story. Risk scores and the 3 month, 1 year and 3 year scenarios are simple math on these numbers, not predictions. Nothing here is financial advice.
